title: The Scope Edge
prompt:
You are leading the passive reconnaissance phase of a penetration test against a mid-sized insurance company. Scope: two domains (insurer.com and insurer-portal.com), two IP ranges (/24 each), and three named web applications. Engagement start date: Monday. Passive recon authorised; active testing begins Thursday.

On Tuesday afternoon, during DNS enumeration of insurer.com, you notice that the CNAME for their developer documentation portal points to insurer.readthedocs.io. You do not investigate readthedocs — it is clearly a third-party hosted service and not in scope.

But then something else catches your attention. While running: site:insurer.com filetype:pdf you discover a PDF titled 'Insurer Group Infrastructure Map v2.1.pdf' — hosted at insurer.com/internal/docs/. The document is publicly accessible and indexed by Google. You open it.

The PDF is a complete internal network diagram. It shows the corporate network, the DMZ, the internal database servers, the VPN gateway, and something unexpected: a third domain — insurer-claims.com — annotated as 'legacy claims processing, scheduled for decommission Q4 2023.' It is now Q3 2026. The domain is not in your scope document.

You run a quick WHOIS lookup on insurer-claims.com (purely passive). It is still registered to the same insurance company. You do not query its DNS or visit any URLs.

You now have:
• A critical finding (internal network diagram publicly accessible)
• Knowledge of a third domain that appears to belong to the client but is not in scope
• A potentially still-active legacy system that is two years past its decommission date

Think through the following questions before the next block reveals the professional response.
guideQuestions: The network diagram is accessible at insurer.com — which is in scope. Is documenting this finding straightforward, or does the nature of the document (a complete internal infrastructure map) change how you handle it?

You ran a WHOIS lookup on insurer-claims.com — a domain not in your scope. Was that a scope violation? What is the distinction between looking up public registration data and actually investigating or testing a system?

insurer-claims.com is strongly implied to belong to the client, may be a live legacy system two years past its decommission date, and is not in scope. What do you do with this information — ignore it, investigate it, or something else?

At what point in this Tuesday afternoon session should you stop what you are doing and contact the client — and who do you contact: the project manager, the technical lead, or the emergency contact named in the Rules of Engagement?
instructorNote: The professional answers: (1) The network diagram is documented as Critical — its existence on a public server is a finding, but it is handled with minimum necessary access: screenshot the Google result and the URL, confirm accessibility (one HTTP request), do not read or extract the infrastructure details beyond what proves the exposure. The content of the diagram is sensitive — reading and using it to expand your investigation of other systems crosses a line. Report it as a critical finding immediately. (2) WHOIS on insurer-claims.com is not a scope violation — WHOIS is a public database query, not a connection to the domain or any of its systems. (3) insurer-claims.com is flagged to the client — verbally and in writing — asking whether they want to expand scope to include it. Do not investigate it without written authorisation. (4) Contact the project manager and cc the emergency contact, as this is a critical finding during business hours — not the emergency contact alone, which would be reserved for active incidents.
